Part 11 Event-Driven Dynamic Projection ​

Dynamic projection starts from a joint state with evidential statuses recorded. It analyzes state differences, transmission, feedback, and branching after observed, reported, planned, hypothetical, or simulated events. Actions that actually occur can change reality with or without authorization. They must all be recorded according to the evidence. Whether an action occurred, how it is evaluated normatively, any legal or institutional authority, and permission to carry it out on this occasion must each be judged separately. Projection must specify which changes can be established directly, which are only conditional consequences, and which signals would support or weaken the corresponding paths.

11Note

Understanding this section

Part Eleven: Event-Driven Dynamic Projection

Dynamic projection is not continuing a fluent story; it asks what is currently known, where an event type changes things first, and through which conditions it affects somewhere else. Begin by preserving the status of facts, hearsay, plans, and model assumptions.

This part starts from a joint state with explicit evidence status. It connects actors, circles, relations, material conditions, and experiential-meaning conditions for a task, without claiming observation of the world’s full state. Every item retains its source, window, support, and unknowns; subsequent inference cannot merge them into equally reliable starting points.

The introduction lists five entry types: observed, reported, planned, hypothetical, and simulated events. Observed events still have measurement-contract limits; a report may truly occur while its content remains unchecked; plans may affect preparation without being executed; hypotheses and simulations support only their conditional consequences. Updating event status with new evidence must retain relations and versions rather than erase original uncertainty.

After an event, distinguish at least directly confirmable state differences, conditional consequences inferred from mechanisms, and signals supporting or weakening the corresponding paths. Receiving a message, for example, is a separately checkable reception event; changed belief, action, or institutional fields require corresponding material. Observing two successive events does not automatically identify the channel between them.

Actual action may change reality even without authorization. Analysis must record actions and consequences that actually occur, separately retaining normative evaluation, legal or institutional authority, and execution permission for this occasion. No right to act does not mean no action; action taken does not confer the right. Recording facts neither excuses the action nor permits the model to implement it.

This connects to §11.3’s notation: u(t) specifically denotes externally authorized actions that actually occur; observed or reported unauthorized actions enter e(t) with their event status and separately recorded authority status. Unperformed unauthorized scenarios may be analyzed while remaining hypothetical or simulated. Separate notation must neither delete reality nor apply the same shock twice.

The following sections set event contracts, joint updating, the nine-step closed loop, propagation and cascades, path graphs, variable candidates, counterfactuals and recursion, stopping, and write-back. Part Twelve then takes responsibility for preregistered foresight and bounded choice. A conditional path obtained now does not establish predictive benefit or authority for real adoption.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Determine the current joint state, evidence cutoff, and gaps; specify whether the task explains, replays, or develops conditional consequences.

  2. 2

    Register one of the five event statuses for each input, separating occurrence of reporting from truth of content.

  3. 3

    Record direct changes, then infer through conditionally supported channels, listing supportive and contrary signals.

  4. 4

    Judge occurrence and authority separately; actual unauthorized events cannot be removed from reality’s record.

  5. 5

    Retain exploratory hypotheses and simulation results at their respective levels without writing them back as actual facts.

  6. 6

    Conditional consequences, future capability, and action authority each carry their own later proof or procedural responsibilities.

Distinctions to keep clear

Action occurs

The corresponding event and consequences exist in the world.

≠

Action authorized

Authority and occasion-specific permission need separate checks; neither implies the other.

A report exists

A person or source actually made a statement.

≠

The report’s contents are true

Requires content verification, not inference from the statement’s existence.

Conditional projection

Possible later states given initial conditions and rules.

≠

Established foresight capability

Additionally needs preregistration, baselines, evaluation, and write-back.

Simulated state

A state generated by model rules.

≠

Real-world observation

A record from actual material, with a different evidence status.

Teaching construction: zero authority while the state actually changesTeaching scenario

AssumptionsDoor, record, and permission are teaching assumptions; no actual door opening, sanction, or legal classification is involved.

A fictional door has state d=0 (closed) at t0; a credible direct record establishes that an actor opens it at t1, giving d=1. A separate explicit premise says the action lacked this occasion’s permission, J=0. Correct recording retains both d:0→1 and J=0 and analyzes it as an observed event. A rule that ‘J=0 makes changing d impossible’ conflicts with the stipulated facts.

BoundaryShows logical independence of fact and authority, not permission to execute unauthorized action.

Logical construction: believing a report does not make it trueTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe listener’s trust is an explicit rule here, not a claim that everyone necessarily believes reports; actual belief change needs separate material.

A fictional report r=1 means a statement ‘the door is open’ was actually received. Actual door state may still be d=0 or d=1. Suppose additionally that the listener initially believed it closed and, under this example’s rule, directly trusts the report, changing belief b from 0 to 1. Both d values fit the same r,b. Report arrival and conditional belief change can therefore be discussed without inventing an open-door fact.

BoundaryReport or belief values cannot directly recover the actual door state.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleNo authorization existed, so the action that actually occurred should not enter the model.

What it limitsMistaking an authority limit for factual nonexistence omits actual risks and consequences.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleThe model generates the same future three times, so it has become an observed outcome.

What it limitsRepeated generation adds model material, not external facts.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • Do not merge unlawfulness or unauthorized-status judgments with whether an action occurred; no case-specific legal judgment is made here.
  • Recording harmful or unauthorized action does not authorize the model to replicate it.
  • Direct observation may also omit or mismeasure; it cannot become an absolute fact of unlimited scope.
  • Generating the same simulation many times adds no new real-world sources.

Scope and open questions

This part’s introduction specifies material status and responsibility boundaries; logical constructions suffice to show nonimplications. Specific historical material appears in later event and path units rather than being forced into normative proof here.

  • This guide executes no real action and obtains no new authority over any actual object.

11.1The Difference Between Projection and Narrative Continuation ​

In briefA story often selects a smooth ending; structural projection must state which other endings fit current material equally well. Its credibility lies not in always sounding certain but in traceable conditions at every step and knowing where to stop when key conditions are missing.

Narrative continuation can choose what comes next by coherence alone. Structural projection must preserve conditions, channels, competing paths, and the meaning of failure. If key variables are missing, the projection should stop at an unknown or generate variable candidates. It must not fill the gaps with the smoothest story. If several continuations are consistent with existing evidence, keep them as separate branches. If paths are incomparable, do not force an ordering.

The minimum inputs to projection are a frozen snapshot, event records, mechanism hypotheses, parameter ranges, a clock policy, a propagation policy, unknowns, and stopping conditions. The minimum outputs are a path graph, state differences at each step, support status, early signals, contrary signals, residuals, variable candidates, and write-back requirements.

InputWhat Must Be FrozenConsequence If Left Unfrozen
Joint snapshotActors, circles[1], relations, M/Ψ, clocks, and evidence cutoffThe starting point is rewritten after the results
EventType, time, source, objects reached, and channelsRumors, plans, and facts are conflated
MechanismDirection, carrier, delay, threshold, and failure conditionsEach outcome can be explained arbitrarily
ParameterValue, interval, level, or explicit unknownFalse precision masks uncertainty
StoppingConditions involving information, risk, exceeding bounds, and resourcesThe story continues indefinitely
11.1Note

Understanding this section

11.1 Projection versus Narrative Continuation

A story often selects a smooth ending; structural projection must state which other endings fit current material equally well. Its credibility lies not in always sounding certain but in traceable conditions at every step and knowing where to stop when key conditions are missing.

Narrative may select one coherent continuation for literary purposes; structural projection on factual tasks cannot treat coherence as support. Preserve conditions, transmission channels, competing paths, and failure meanings: what permits continuation, which observation refutes, and which gap leaves judgment unresolved. More branches are not inherently better, but grounded differences cannot be flattened by a fluent story.

Minimum input has eight items: frozen snapshot, event records, mechanism hypotheses, parameter ranges, clock policy, propagation policy, unknowns, and stopping conditions. Freezing identifies the version used in this run, not absolute correctness. Explicit unknowns may also be frozen. Late material creates a new run rather than flowing backward into the old starting point.

The joint snapshot freezes actors, circles, relations, M/Ψ, clocks, and evidence cutoff, preventing post-result object changes or access to future information. M and Ψ separately retain material and experience–meaning conditions. Genuinely inapplicable items may have reasons stated; symmetrical forms do not justify invented psychological states.

Events freeze type, time, source, reached objects, and channels, preventing rumors, plans, observations, and simulations from being mixed. Mechanisms freeze direction, carrier, delay, threshold, and failure conditions, preventing an explanation from retrospectively reshaping itself for every result. If only a candidate mechanism is available, say candidate; the procedural act of freezing cannot promote it to causal fact.

Parameters may be points, intervals, grades, or explicitly unknown, depending on material and task. Intervals do not automatically carry probability distributions, nor do two branches automatically split equally. Clock policy specifies sequence, update rhythm, and concurrency handling; propagation policy specifies transmissible channels and blocking conditions, rather than allowing every node to update simultaneously after one event.

Stopping conditions cover insufficient information, risk, use beyond scope, and resource limits. A local channel gap pauses dependent inferences, while independently established direct facts or bounded total effects may remain. Failure of shared premises or overall use conditions stops all relevant runs. Stopping does not force unknown into failure or erase known facts.

Minimum output also has eight items: path graph, state differences at each step, support status, early signals, contrary signals, residuals, variable candidates, and write-back requirements. The graph shows grounded subsequent differences; state differences specify fields; support status distinguishes factual and conditional status; the two signal types strengthen and weaken paths respectively, rather than collecting only favorable news.

Residuals are differences unexplained by the current representation and mechanism, not arbitrary random noise or immediately nameable hidden motives. Variable candidates turn gaps into testable questions. Write-back requirements specify when and from which sources results are appended, how original branches, competing paths, and baselines are compared, and how failures remain recorded.

If material permits several continuations, retain parallel branches. Without grounded probabilities or rankings, do not force an ordering. Consequence severity or a tight observation window may prioritize investigation of one branch, but research priority is not occurrence probability. Clear supported scope is stronger than unsupported decimals or directions creating an impression of certainty.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Freeze eight input categories, declaring each item's factual, candidate, scenario, or unknown status.

  2. 2

    Specify the table's five content groups—joint snapshot, events, mechanisms, parameters, and stopping—and additionally expand clock and propagation policies.

  3. 3

    Generate state differences stepwise from the starting point under explicit rules, not narrative order in place of channels.

  4. 4

    Retain grounded competing branches and incomparable items, listing early and contrary signals separately.

  5. 5

    Register unexplained differences as residuals and several distinguishable candidates, without inventing actual values.

  6. 6

    Pause only paths affected by a gap, or stop all relevant runs when shared premises or overall use conditions fail.

  7. 7

    Append actual outcomes under predetermined requirements and evaluate old runs; new information cannot rewrite old success.

Distinctions to keep clear

Frozen input

Identifies this run's version, knowns, and unknowns.

≠

True or sufficient input

Still requires evidence and applicability checks; freezing is not certification.

Candidate mechanism

Testable hypotheses about direction, carriers, and conditions.

≠

Identified mechanism

Requires corresponding distinguishing material, not inference from narrative coherence.

Branch interval

A range of still-compatible values or continuations.

≠

Probability distribution

Needs generation or calibration grounds; two branches are not automatically 50% each.

Research priority

Consequences, timing, or distinguishability determine what to examine first.

≠

Path-probability ranking

Asks which is likelier and requires separate evidence.

Local stopping

Stops extending the part dependent on a missing condition.

≠

Erasing every result

Independent facts and results may remain.

Mathematical construction: retain two queue paths from one starting pointTeaching scenario

AssumptionsHomogeneous tasks, a work-conserving service rule, fixed c, no hidden entries/exits, and common within-window order are explicit. Numbers are teaching constructions.

Let fictional q0=2 items, with 1 additional arrival at t0. Each window first adds registered new tasks, then a single service point processes exactly min(queue,c) items. Capacity c remains fixed over two windows but is known only as c∈{1,2}; there are no new arrivals in window two. Thus q1=max(0,2+1−c). For c=1, q1=2 and q2=1; for c=2, q1=1 and q2=0. Both paths fit the starting point. A smooth story of “definitely empty next window” cannot be selected, nor may each branch receive 50% without probability material. Actual first-window completions distinguish the branches.

BoundaryIf first-window records show 3 completions or a queue greater than 2, at least one original condition needs review. c cannot quietly be changed while retaining success of the original run.

Teaching construction: late information creates a new versionTeaching scenario

AssumptionsDates, records, and credibility are teaching assumptions, not actual research logs.

Fictional V1 closes information at noon Monday, knowing only c∈{1,2}. Tuesday brings a credible record establishing actual Monday c=2, allowing reconstruction of the past and creation of V2. V1 retains its contemporaneous two branches and unknown. Backfilling V2's c=2 into V1 and claiming a unique Monday prediction of an empty queue rewrites the starting point after results.

BoundaryRetrospective explanation may be valuable, but its information set differs from the original foresight evaluation.

Snow retained the decline before pump-handle removalDocumented case

In the 1855 second edition, Snow records removal of the Broad Street pump handle on September 8, 1854, while explicitly noting that incidence had already declined markedly before use of the water stopped and discussing population departures. The history cannot therefore be reduced to “decline began only after handle removal.”

SourceJohn Snow, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera, 1855 second editionOriginal printed pp.51–52: onset-date discussion following Table I and the passage beginning “The pump-well in Broad Street, Golden Square”Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsTable I compiles onset and death information for eventual fatalities, not a curve of all infections. This section estimates no independent removal effect, nor infers complete ineffectiveness from insufficient identification. The book is retrospective and does not establish that this lesson reconstructed the complete information set available then.

What does not follow

  • Complete methodological fields, complete diagrams, and freezing itself are not real-world truth.
  • Do not choose for actors, supply inner states, or invent new variable values to complete a narrative.
  • Unknown parameters may support conditional ranges without supporting directions or rankings.
  • Retrospective reconstruction cannot masquerade as contemporaneously available information or a successful prediction made before results.
  • An unidentified additional effect is not zero effect and does not cancel independently established evidence for other questions.

Scope and open questions

The same primary narrative explicitly preserves pretrends and competing conditions, directly showing why structural projection cannot select only a smooth retrospective chain. This section offers no current medical advice.

  • No complete historical counterfactual comparison was obtained. The additional handle-removal effect remains outside this example's identification scope, and the queue construction provides no effect evidence for historical data.

For c=1 and c=2, what are queue lengths after two windows?

Respectively 1 and 0, calculated window by window under work-conserving updates. Retain both when only the starting range is known.

If Monday's capacity record arrives Tuesday, may it be backfilled into Monday's old forecast to claim a contemporaneous hit?

No. A new version or replay may be created, but the old information cutoff remains.

If only one intermediate channel is unknown while endpoint change was directly observed, should the endpoint fact be deleted?

No. Retain direct change or independently identified results, limiting only the unsupported propagation explanation.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

What can be done when branches cannot be ranked?

State scope and unknowns, give distinguishing observations, conditions, contrary signals, and stopping points. Research priority may have separately explicit reasons.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Does freezing a mechanism hypothesis prove it?

No. Freezing supplies an evaluation reference; mechanism truth still requires corresponding evidence.

11.2The Event Contract[2] ​

In brief“Occurred,” “someone says it occurred,” “planned,” and “suppose it occurred” have very different implications for the next judgment. An event contract gives each input a status card so a retold claim cannot become an unverified fact after repeated transmission.

There are five kinds of event: observed, reported, planned, hypothetical, and simulated. The type must be included in the record. A reported event can affect people who believe it but must not automatically be treated as having occurred. A plan may change expectations without amounting to execution. A hypothetical event serves conditional analysis. A simulated event belongs only to a model run and must not be written back as a fact about reality.

An event record must include at least the event ID, time or window of occurrence, time of observation, source, affected actors, affected circles, channels, direct changes, evidential status, disputes, competing explanations, reversibility, duration, and subsequent observations.

Event TypePermitted Uses in ProjectionFactual StatusRequired Limits
ObservedExplanation, replay, and forward projectionHolds within the observation contractSources, omissions, and measurement error
ReportedPropagation of belief and conditional projectionThat a report was made does not establish that its contents are trueThe reporting party’s position, verification, and disputes
PlannedExpectations, preparations, and strategic interactionExistence of the plan does not establish executionAuthorization, resources, and conditions for cancellation
HypotheticalCounterfactuals and scenario comparisonNo factual status in realityConditions, purpose, and feasibility
SimulatedUnfolding paths within the modelModel state onlyModel version, parameters, and prohibition on extrapolation
11.2Note

Understanding this section

11.2 Event contract

“Occurred,” “someone says it occurred,” “planned,” and “suppose it occurred” have very different implications for the next judgment. An event contract gives each input a status card so a retold claim cannot become an unverified fact after repeated transmission.

The five event types distinguish use and evidential status, not a low-to-high credibility ranking. One real process may produce different records: publication of a plan is a real publication event, while its future action remains unexecuted; publication of a simulation report is a real transmission event, while its internal failure does not thereby become real. Distinguish the recorded objects, cross-referencing when necessary without duplicating impacts.

Observed events may enter explanation, replay, and forward projection, but only within their observation contracts. Sources, observation positions, omissions, and measurement errors are required. Seeing “complete” on a screen directly supports that display or record; external execution still needs task-appropriate execution material. Visible interfaces are not categorically invalid: the observed field determines the evidence ceiling.

Reported events permit analysis of belief propagation and conditional paths. The report's occurrence may be established while content truth remains under review. Reporter position, accessible information, disputes, and source lineage matter; repeated forwarding is not multiple independent witnesses. Reports may change recipient expectations, but actual reach and belief need evidence; identical reactions cannot be prescribed for everyone.

Planned events may change preparation, resource reservations, and strategic interaction without meaning the future action is complete. Register proposer, object, planned time, authorization, resources, and cancellation conditions. Approved plans may remain unexecuted because of resources or subsequent events; unapproved plans may genuinely affect expectations. Register plan existence, execution authority, and actual occurrence separately.

Hypothetical events serve counterfactual and scenario comparisons, requiring conditions, purpose, and feasibility. Conditions may distinguish mechanisms without claiming actual permission or inevitability. Infeasible scenarios used as logical boundaries must retain that status rather than become actual recommendations.

Simulated events belong only to specified model runs, requiring model version, initial conditions, parameters, and prohibited-extrapolation boundaries. Calculated trajectories expose conditional consequences, but repeated sampling still comes from the same model. Without new external material, it cannot raise the evidential status of a claim that a real event occurred.

Fourteen minimum-record items each bear responsibility: event ID preserves reference; occurrence time/window locates the object event; observation time states when it became known; source supplies grounds; affected actors and affected circles separately retain scope; channel explains reach; direct change specifies actual altered fields; evidence status marks support and unknowns; disputes retain inconsistent material; competing explanations prevent a single-story monopoly; reversibility distinguishes what can be undone; duration prevents extrapolation from an instant; subsequent observation specifies review. Event type must also remain explicit, not hidden in narrative tone.

Occurrence time may be an interval or a report's claimed time; invent no precise timestamp. Observation time differs from occurrence time, and §11.3.2 additionally distinguishes model-entry time. Late material may revise today's understanding of the past, but cannot give past forecasts records unavailable then.

Affected objects are not automatically “everyone relevant.” A message reaching a department does not establish every member read it; changed quantity fields do not establish changed trust, authority, and relations. Reversibility also has multiple dimensions: replenishable resources do not mean transmitted information, elapsed deadlines, and damaged trust can be fully restored.

After verification supplies new material, append sources and correction relationships and revisit branches depending on the content. Later falsity of content does not erase the report's occurrence or actual effects; later truth does not erase its then-unverified status in earlier evaluations. None of this analysis independently authorizes real collection, experiments, or interventions.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First identify the recorded object and its five-way status. An actual publication/report event and its content may have different factual statuses.

  2. 2

    Complete the fourteen minimum record items and explicitly add the type; preserve unknown fields honestly.

  3. 3

    Record occurrence, observation, and necessary model-entry times separately; also separate permissions, resources, and execution.

  4. 4

    Limit eligible projections and evidential ceilings by type; simulated states are not actual observations.

  5. 5

    Verify sources and disputes, distinguish forwarding from independent witnessing, and avoid applying an event repeatedly.

  6. 6

    Append relationships for content corrections, updating dependent branches separately while preserving the report's own consequences.

  7. 7

    Design later observations only within necessity, privacy, and authorization limits; analytical need creates no permission.

Distinctions to keep clear

Observed record

Information obtained under specified observation rules.

≠

Complete actual state

May contain unobserved fields, errors, and hidden changes.

Plan approved

A permission or decision has been established.

≠

Plan executed

Still requires actual-action and outcome records.

Report content false

Corresponding counterevidence supports falsity; mere lack of support remains unverified or unresolved.

≠

Report did not occur

The report and its propagation effects may still be real.

Hypothetical event

A conditional object stipulated by the analyst.

≠

Simulated event

An internal update in a model run. Neither is a real-world observation.

Recoverable resources

A specified quantity can be replenished through later action.

≠

Completely reversible event

Deadline, propagation, and relational consequences may be irrecoverable.

Teaching construction: five statuses for the same “decrease of 4 items”Teaching scenario

AssumptionsInventory units, correct counting, no other changes, and only two report possibilities are explicit construction premises; no actual warehouse or experiment is involved.

Suppose fictional initial inventory is 10 items with no other inflows or outflows. Correct direct counting confirms removal of 4, yielding 6. If only an unverified report says “4 removed,” and this example allows only truth or falsity with no removal when false, inventory belongs to {6,10}. If removal of 4 is planned for tomorrow, current inventory remains 10; only the conditional post-execution value is 6. Hypothetical removal yields conditional consequence 6; a simulator calculating 6 under the same rule produces only a model value. Identical numbers do not confer identical evidential status.

BoundaryAn unverified report cannot automatically yield mean 8 because no truth probabilities are supplied; simulated output 6 is not actual inventory 6.

Teaching event card: separating claimed time from observation timeTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAll IDs, people, times, and permission scopes are teaching constructions, never actual event cards or valid authorization documents.

Fictional ID=Toy-E1, type=reported; claimed occurrence day 1 at 09:00, report received at 10:00, model entry at 10:05; source=fictional team message Toy-S1; affected actor=fictional custodian A, circle=fictional warehouse group W; channel=received team message; direct change=message received, physical inventory awaiting verification; evidence status=report exists, content unverified; dispute=stocktake incomplete; competing explanations=actual removal or message error; reversibility=stock can be replenished, but propagated information cannot be presumed fully retractable; duration=removal and effect duration unknown; subsequent observation=check stocktake and withdrawal records within this example's permitted scope.

BoundaryA completed card does not prove its content; the direct change cannot be written as an established inventory reduction of 4.

Set construction: two forwards do not add two physical shocksTeaching scenario

AssumptionsMessage lineage and one withdrawal are stipulated here. Actual deduplication requires evidence; textual similarity alone cannot justify merging.

A fictional original message about removal of 4 items is forwarded twice; all three materials refer to one candidate event. If eventually verified as one removal, inventory changes 10→6. Applying a reduction of 4 for every message yields −2, duplicating the shock and potentially violating inventory bounds. If two independent withdrawals actually occurred, create separate events and verify their times and quantities.

BoundaryMaterial counts differ from event counts, but deduplication needs cannot cancel actual repeated events.

Submission, use, and approval in Maryland's administrative reportDocumented case

Printed p.9 of Maryland's 2024 report separately records submission of a mitigation plan to CMS on September 13, 2023, use of the updated automatic-renewal system process beginning in November 2023, and CMS approval in February 2024. This section retains all three as distinct events and windows. Actual use rests on the report's explicit statement, not automatic inference from plan submission.

SourceMaryland Department of Health, FY2024 fourth-quarter renewal review report, April 2024Medicaid Mitigation of Ex Parte Renewals, printed p.9, measure 3 and the “updated ex parte systems process” paragraph after measure 5Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThis lesson relies on an official retrospective administrative report, not firsthand system observation. Month-level times are not expanded into invented dates. The three times do not independently establish illegality or absent authority before approval, or all coverage, treatment, or health consequences. Only 2023–2024 historical material is explained.

What does not follow

  • The five statuses are not a ladder automatically climbed with retelling count.
  • Check observational credibility under its contract. Report count cannot replace independent sources.
  • Plan publication, approval, resource preparation, execution, and effects are distinct events. Retain windows when precise dates are unavailable.
  • Actual unauthorized actions must still be recorded; simulating an action creates no execution authority.
  • Complete fields supply a checkable structure, not a guarantee that every fact is true or all required material is present.

Scope and open questions

The same page explicitly distinguishes institutional events and times, making it suitable for checking non-equivalence among plan existence, actual execution, and approval; it provides no current eligibility or legal advice.

  • The administrative report does not supply all individual execution logs, arrival records, or health consequences for this lesson; those fields remain unchecked. No complete legal authorization chain for the plan is invented.

11.3The Joint State Update Formula ​

In briefThe update equation is a responsibility checklist: the states, events, actions, disturbances, assumptions, and history used at this step should each be traceable. Writing F does not discover the world's unique operating formula; putting unknowns inside symbols cannot pretend to explain them.

The joint state can be written as follows.

Ω(t) = <A(t), C(t), R(t), M(t), Ψ(t), Q(t), E≤t, SP(t), W(t), K(t)>.

An update can be written as follows.

Ω(t+Δ) = F[Ω(t), e(t), u(t), ξ(t) | θ, h].

Here e(t) is the event, u(t) is an externally authorized action that actually occurred, ξ(t) is an exogenous disturbance or unmodeled residual, θ denotes the frozen hypotheses about mechanisms and parameters, and h is the historical term. The formula specifies only what must be recorded. It does not assert that there is a unique true F, and the function symbol must not be used in place of specific mechanisms.

Observed violations, actions beyond authorization, refusals to carry out orders, and unauthorized acts in another’s stead are recorded as observed/reported events under e(t) with their evidence. The actor, consequences, and status of their authority must be recorded separately. The lack of authority must not be grounds for deleting an event from the factual record. Violations that have not occurred enter only hypothetical/simulated branches. The definition of u(t) still requires authorization and actual occurrence. Feasibility in a scenario does not amount to permission in reality. 〔Studies 15.08, 21.03, 21.08, 28.06, 32.08〕

Each update must distinguish directly observed state differences, inferences supported by the mechanism contract, scenario values set to explore a path, and residuals still unexplained. All four retain their provenance in subsequent paths. Appearing together in a snapshot does not give them the same evidential status.

11.3Note

Understanding this section

11.3 Joint-State Update Equation

The update equation is a responsibility checklist: the states, events, actions, disturbances, assumptions, and history used at this step should each be traceable. Writing F does not discover the world's unique operating formula; putting unknowns inside symbols cannot pretend to explain them.

The original joint state is Ω(t)=<A(t),C(t),R(t),M(t),Ψ(t),Q(t),E≤t,SP(t),W(t),K(t)>. A retains actors, C circles, R relations, M and Ψ material and experiential-meaning conditions respectively, Q channel constraints, E≤t events through the corresponding time, SP scale profiles, W evidence, and K identity criteria. It is a task-relevant representation, not omniscient access to every variable in the world.

The update is Ω(t+Δ)=F[Ω(t),e(t),u(t),ξ(t)|θ,h]. Δ is the declared progression interval; e is an event; u is an externally authorized action that actually occurred; ξ is an exogenous disturbance or unmodeled residual; θ is frozen mechanisms and parameters; h is a historical term. Each may have internal structure. The function symbol means only “the next step depends on these inputs”; actual rules, parameters, scope, and evidence cannot be omitted.

F is not claimed to be the unique true function. Different mechanisms may be equivalent on current material, and some parameters may have only intervals. Retain multiple candidates, ranges, or unknowns rather than disguising one computed output as the unique real consequence. Specify which terms are observable, inferred, or scenario assumptions only.

The definition of u is a recording convention; it cannot make unauthorized actions disappear from reality. Observed or reported violations, overreach, refusal to execute, or unauthorized proxy action enter e with corresponding event status, separately recording actors, consequences, and permission status. Violations not yet occurring belong only to hypothetical or simulated branches. Factual occurrence, normative judgment, and execution permission remain separate. An actual action referenced in several fields still applies its corresponding state effect only once.

ξ cannot become a universal black box for things one prefers not to explain. Preserve sources and scopes for identified exogenous disturbances; if it is only an unexplained residual, retain that status. Random-error models need grounds. Missing records, refusal to disclose, and unmodeled mechanisms cannot all be called zero-mean noise. Nor does writing h into a formula establish additional historical effects; current-carrier effects and G3 historical increments beyond the current representation still require separate evidence routes.

Each step's outputs distinguish at least four statuses: directly observed state differences, inferences supported by mechanism contracts, exploratory scenario values, and unexplained residuals. All may coexist in Ω without transferring evidential status to one another. A simulated future used as the next round's input retains its conditions and unknowns; it cannot be renamed current reality.

The parent section specifies update symbols and status responsibilities. Section 11.3.1 further separates actual states, observation rules, and identification sets, explaining when existing material suffices for a bounded question. Section 11.3.2 manages three times, late material, source corrections, and concurrent ordering. Together they constrain updating, not add automatic truth certification to F.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Register Ω's ten components individually, with task, scale, evidence, and K; state whether unlisted fields are irrelevant, omitted, or unknown.

  2. 2

    Write the F and θ actually used, specifying Δ, input sources, ranges, and failure conditions.

  3. 3

    Distinguish e and u by definition. Actual unauthorized actions enter events rather than being deleted; repeated references do not apply them repeatedly.

  4. 4

    Declare ξ and h statuses and the effects they can support. Unknowns do not default to randomness, nor history to G3 support.

  5. 5

    Preserve each step's observed, inferred, scenario, and residual state differences separately.

  6. 6

    Retain multiple Fs or output ranges where needed, constrained by identification sets and event-continuation rules.

Distinctions to keep clear

The symbolic position F

Specifies dependencies and recording responsibilities.

≠

The actual mechanism has been found

Still requires concrete rules, discriminating evidence, and an applicability domain.

u

An externally authorized action that actually occurred.

≠

Actual unauthorized actions within e

May still change reality and are registered as observed/reported.

Unmodeled residual

A difference left unexplained by the current account.

≠

Random noise

Has a corresponding probabilistic meaning only under an appropriate error model.

Historical input h

A record position whose content and use must be specified.

≠

Historical increment established

Separately requires incremental evidence beyond the current representation; symbols do not create it.

Four statuses of state differences

Observed, supported inference, scenario value, and residual, each with a separate trail.

≠

Same snapshot, same truth status

Coexistence in Ω does not give them equal evidential status.

Mathematical construction: preserving event status and output ranges within one update equationTeaching scenario

AssumptionsUnits match, events are counted once, and no other inflows/outflows exist. h has no separate effect in this local model; the ξ set is a teaching assumption, not an estimated real distribution.

Let fictional resources s0=5 units, with confirmed but unauthorized consumption e=−2 and authorized replenishment that actually arrives u=+1. Freeze the local rule s1=s0+e+u+ξ, explicitly allowing only two unknown extra-loss scenarios ξ∈{0,−1}, hence s1∈{4,3}. If extra loss is unverified, this output range is a conditional model result, not observed resources of 3. Nor may e be deleted because consumption was unauthorized, yielding 6 or 5.

BoundaryThe example does not treat all events as linearly additive or authorize actual resource transfers.

Logical construction: identical observations can still admit different FsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe two rules are only a finite candidate set; actual models may be more numerous. All dynamics have not been estimated from one datum.

Suppose only one transition x0=1, x1=2 is observed. Both F_A(x)=x+1 and F_B(x)=2x fit it, but next yield 3 and 4 respectively. Without additional conditions, calling either the “unique true F” exceeds the material. Retain both candidates and seek subsequent records capable of distinguishing them.

BoundaryIdentical current fit guarantees neither identical next steps nor equal one-half real-world probabilities for the models.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleΩ and F are fully written, so the model has read every state in the world.

What it limitsComplete symbols specify only a representational interface; they do not guarantee complete observations, mechanisms, or hidden variables.

Teaching counterexampleCalling all deviations ξ and all persistence h validates the model.

What it limitsNaming provides neither error-model nor historical-identification evidence; preserve counterexamples and unknowns.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • Formal completeness is not completeness of the world; a computable function does not prove a correct mechanism.
  • Do not force unknown parameters into point values or upgrade simulated continuations into real facts.
  • Keep factual records of actual unauthorized events without using analysis to carry out the action.
  • If a total effect has been independently identified, retain its bounded result; lack of unique identification of the internal F does not erase it.
  • ξ and h must not absorb every counterexample and make the model incapable of failure.

Scope and open questions

This unit formally explains an update equation and input statuses. Explicit constructions check non-implications; historical cases cannot prove a unique F exists. Specific observation and event questions appear in the two subsections.

  • Actual F, θ, ξ ranges, and h effects each require material; this mathematical construction estimates no real system parameters.

11.3.1States, Observations, and Identified Sets ​

In briefWe obtain records, not the world itself. The key is not whether every hidden variable can be guessed, but whether all situations still compatible with the records already give the same answer to the current question.

A joint snapshot is a structured representation of the material currently available. It does not directly read every state of the world. Let z(t) denote the actual state yet to be inferred for the current task, and o(t) the record produced by observation rule H, sampling positions, and conditions of data collection. It can be written as o(t)=H[z(t),m(t),ε(t)]. m(t) includes who can enter the record, when they are measured, and which fields are withheld from disclosure for protection. ε(t) is used only when there is a corresponding error model. Unknowns must not all be called random noise. When conditions allow, numerical measurements can use additive error. Text and categorical records use their corresponding generation rules. Ω should preserve the distinction between the records and the judgments, so a change in observation rule is not mistaken for a change in the object.

The same set of records can correspond to several states or mechanisms. Let Z(o) denote the set of states still compatible with the record under the stated model and error bounds. If the answer to question q is the same in every state in Z(o), the current material is sufficient for the question. A limited answer can be given without recovering every latent variable. If the values differ, the output should retain their range, any direction that can be identified, or the parts that genuinely remain unknown. Failure to detect a difference in a finite sample does not automatically establish that only one answer remains over the entire set.

The set also helps plan the next observation. First identify state distinctions that would change the current answer or the comparison of actions. Then check which feasible observations could distinguish them. More precision that leaves the answer unchanged need not help. A low-cost observation that narrows an important branch may be more valuable than expanding the whole variable table. Data collection remains subject to purpose, necessity, and protection. A need for identification does not confer permission to collect data.

11.3.1Note

Understanding this section

11.3.1 States, Observations, and Identification Sets

We obtain records, not the world itself. The key is not whether every hidden variable can be guessed, but whether all situations still compatible with the records already give the same answer to the current question.

Let z(t) denote the actual state to be inferred and o(t) the obtained record, with observation rule o(t)=H[z(t),m(t),ε(t)]. H describes record generation; m includes who can enter the record, when measurement occurs, and which fields are protected from disclosure; ε is used only with a corresponding error model. Selection, protective missingness, and unknown mechanisms cannot all be lumped into random measurement error.

Numerical data may use additive error under appropriate conditions, while text and categories follow their record-generation rules. If observation coverage expands from half to all, record counts may rise while object counts remain unchanged; changed coding rules may also alter category frequencies. Ω must distinguish object changes from changes in how we observe them.

Given an explicit model and permitted errors, Z(o) is the set of states still compatible with the record. It is neither an unspecified confidence interval nor automatically an equal-probability distribution over states. Changing the model or error range changes the set; reported answers must retain this conditional status.

For task question q, if q takes the same value on every state in Z(o), the evidence suffices to answer this bounded question even if many components of z remain unidentified. If values differ, retain the range, identifiable direction, or genuinely unknown parts. Direction cannot be assumed either: if both positive and negative values remain compatible, do not force a direction merely to ‘say something.’

This is not ‘no difference found in the sample means everything is identical.’ Finite samples, measurement noise, and model limits may make differences hard to detect. Claiming a common answer across the set requires proving its range under model constraints or appropriate sufficiency, equivalence, and sensitivity support. Nonsignificance cannot directly become zero effect or sufficient identification.

The next observation should prioritize state differences that would change the current answer or action comparison. If the task asks only for a total, knowing exact container proportions may be unnecessary; if it asks whether both endpoints have a minimum reserve, distribution matters. The same evidence's value changes with the question; no variable table is eternally most complete and necessary.

Observation design remains constrained by purpose, necessity, privacy, and protection. Being able to identify a state does not confer authority to collect corresponding personal information. Without filling every latent variable, there may already be a commonly acceptable action; or the answer may be sufficient while no feasible action exists. Sufficient conditions for action are separately addressed in §12.10.1; authorization cannot be silently completed here.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Declare z, H, m, and the applicable error model, separating actual state from record generation.

  2. 2

    Construct Z(o) under these conditions, retaining unidentified components without assuming probabilities.

  3. 3

    Write the current question as q(z), and calculate or establish its range across the entire compatible set.

  4. 4

    Give a bounded answer when all agree; otherwise retain ranges/directions/unknowns. Failure to detect a finite-sample difference is not proof of identical answers.

  5. 5

    Select the minimal observation that changes the answer or option comparison, rather than increasing precision indiscriminately.

  6. 6

    Check observational purpose, risk, and authority; information needs do not generate permission to collect.

Distinctions to keep clear

z: actual state

The world state the task seeks to infer.

≠

o: observational record

Generated by rules, selection, timing, and error conditions.

The question is identified

q gives the same answer across compatible states.

≠

The full state is recovered

Requires uniqueness of all relevant hidden variables, often unnecessary for the task.

Set-valued range

The possible answer range under an explicit model.

≠

Probability or confidence

Additionally requires a corresponding probability model and inferential procedure.

No difference detected

Limited evidence reveals no difference.

≠

Sufficiency or equivalence established

Requires corresponding rules, tolerance, and sensitivity; there is no automatic upgrade.

An observation is informative

It may narrow current branches.

≠

Authority to observe

Also requires purpose, protection, and authority conditions.

Mathematical construction: a known total with an unknown distributionTeaching scenario

AssumptionsNo omissions, error-free total measurement, exactly two containers, and fixed integer units are all teaching assumptions.

Two fictional containers hold nonnegative integer amounts x and y, with correct total record o=x+y=10 and no other information. Z(o)={(0,10),(1,9),…,(10,0)} has 11 points. The total question q1=x+y is always 10 and already answerable; first-container quantity q2=x ranges from 0 to 10; difference q3=x−y ranges from −10 to 10 with both signs, so direction is unknown. Knowing x is unnecessary for recognizing total 10.

BoundaryIf the real total itself has measurement error, enlarge the compatible set; constant 10 cannot carry over.

Mathematical construction: choose less observation according to the questionTeaching scenario

AssumptionsError-free observation and permission for the check are constructed premises, not authority for real data collection; actual equipment costs are not compared.

Continuing the example, change the task to ‘does each container hold at least 3 units?’ Since y=10−x, this is equivalent to 3≤x≤7. If a permitted check in this example reliably returns the Boolean ‘is x in [3,7]?’ it answers the task without measuring x exactly. If the task changes to how long each container will last, that Boolean information may be insufficient.

BoundaryInformation sufficiency is question-relative; the Boolean record cannot be called sufficient for every later task.

Mathematical construction: the observation rule changes while the object does notTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe proportion is this example's exact record-generation rule; actual random sample counts are not equated to their expectations.

Let true object count z stay at 20, with model recording rule o=mz. Coverage m changes from 1/2 to 1 without other error, so the record changes 10→20 while the true count stays 20. If only o=10 is observed and m∈{1/2,1} is known, z may be 20 or 10. Both growing records and identical records require interpretation through coverage rules.

BoundaryThis does not rule out actual growth; it only refutes the claim that record changes necessarily equal object changes.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleThe total is 10 but the distribution is unknown, so no question can be answered.

What it limitsThe total question has the same answer on all 11 states; a bounded answer can hold.

Teaching counterexampleThe sample difference is nonsignificant, so compatible mechanisms are identical for every question.

What it limitsNondetection does not establish a common answer across the set; sufficient grounds specific to the question and tolerance are required.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleRecord counts doubled, so the true object count must have doubled.

What it limitsChanging coverage rules alone produces the same record pattern in this construction.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • Unlisted states may exist beyond the model's domain; set-based answers retain modeling boundaries.
  • Text, categories, refusal to disclose, and selective records do not all admit additive noise.
  • An identifiable total and unidentified distribution can coexist without canceling each other.
  • If compatible answers include positive and negative directions, direction is also unknown.
  • ‘Wanting to recover the entire state’ does not justify demanding unnecessary or unauthorized information.

Scope and open questions

This section formally argues about observation mappings and identified sets. Three explicit constructions directly test sufficiency for different questions; real cases lacking complete observation contracts are not forced into service as proofs of set identification.

  • A real Z(o) requires actual H, selection processes, and error ranges; this lesson has no complete measurement model for a specific object.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    Given only nonnegative integers x+y=10, how many elements does Z contain, and what can be said about the total and the difference's direction?

  2. 2

    Why does the Boolean check 3≤x≤7 suffice to determine whether both containers have at least 3?

  3. 3

    If coverage rises from half to all while the true count stays 20, why does the record change from 10 to 20?

  4. 4

    Does uniquely identifying a state justify collecting all personal information?

Given only nonnegative integers x+y=10, how many elements does Z contain, and what can be said about the total and the difference's direction?

11 elements. Total 10 is identified; the difference ranges from −10 to 10, with unknown direction.

Why does the Boolean check 3≤x≤7 suffice to determine whether both containers have at least 3?

If coverage rises from half to all while the true count stays 20, why does the record change from 10 to 20?

Does uniquely identifying a state justify collecting all personal information?

No. Information needs do not confer collection authority, and the current task may require only a bounded distinction.

11.3.2Event Processing and State Continuation ​

In briefA new message may mean the world just changed, or that today we learned what happened yesterday. An updating system must separate those cases while handling corrections, repeated relays, and order conflicts, without replacing actual event order with message-arrival order.

Each input retains the time of the event, the time the record was obtained, and the time it entered the model. Material that arrives late can change what is now known about the past, but it cannot rewrite the information set available at the time. When correcting a source, append the link to the correction and recompute the states and paths that depend on that source. Retain local results that do not depend on it. When multiple sources recount one event, retain those sources and a single candidate identity for the event to avoid applying the same shock more than once. Events with similar descriptions must not be merged without verification.

State updating consists of two operations. An evidence update revises the judgment about z(t). Advancing the mechanism estimates the change from z(t) to a subsequent state. A credible record that “work stopped yesterday” is an evidence update today. The stoppage itself belongs to yesterday’s real events. Rerunning a model and obtaining another response that work “may have stopped” adds only simulated material. Both kinds of update can change Ω, but their reasons and evidential statuses must be kept separate.

Concurrent events may be combined in any order only if the operations commute, shared resources are not in conflict, and neither changes the other’s conditions. If two actions compete for a resource, overwrite the same record, or change each other’s available action set, retain branches for the possible orders or specify an explicit rule for concurrency. Similar timestamps do not establish simultaneity. The order in which execution calls return does not by itself reveal the causal order of real events.

11.3.2Note

Understanding this section

11.3.2 Event handling and state continuation

A new message may mean the world just changed, or that today we learned what happened yesterday. An updating system must separate those cases while handling corrections, repeated relays, and order conflicts, without replacing actual event order with message-arrival order.

Retain three times for every input: event occurrence, record acquisition, and model entry. Occurrence may be known only as a window or a reported claim; do not invent exact seconds. Late evidence can change current judgments about the past, but the information available then cannot be rewritten, or replay will masquerade as prediction made at the time.

For corrected sources, append the correction relationship and recalculate states and paths depending on that source. Dependencies determine recalculation scope; unrelated conclusions are not all revoked. Retain old versions so the basis of the original judgment and where it failed remain visible.

Multiple items may relay the same event. Retain multiple sources with one candidate event identity to avoid applying the shock repeatedly. Similar wording may also describe distinct events; similar names alone cannot merge them. The times, objects, sources, and event identities supporting deduplication may themselves remain unchecked.

Evidence updating revises knowledge of z(t); mechanism advancement estimates changes from time t onward. If a credible record that ‘work stopped yesterday’ arrives today, today's events are learning and updating model evidence; the stoppage belongs to yesterday. Rerunning a model to obtain ‘work may stop’ produces only new simulation material, not an actual work-stoppage event.

Both operations may change Ω, but for different reasons. More accurate knowledge of yesterday's inventory is not another warehouse delivery today; projecting future inventory by an explicit rule is not seeing the future. The same state field can therefore carry both an object time and a knowledge version.

Concurrent events can be combined in arbitrary order only if operations commute, shared resources do not conflict, and neither changes the other's conditions. Check commutation on the relevant complete state and permitted domain; identical final totals alone do not establish identical authority, resource occupation, or intermediate harm.

When two actions compete for capacity, overwrite the same record, or change each other's available actions, retain order branches or explicit concurrency rules. Nearby timestamps do not establish simultaneity, and an executor returning first does not establish earlier real occurrence; transmission and processing delays may differ. If order is unidentified, output the corresponding result set rather than secretly choosing an order for reproducibility.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    For every input, distinguish occurrence, acquisition, and model-entry times, including precision and evidence.

  2. 2

    Treat new evidence as knowledge updating, register real events at their object time, and separately retain conditional status for model advancement.

  3. 3

    Append source corrections and recalculate along dependencies, retaining independent local results and old versions.

  4. 4

    Check candidate event identity for deduplication, neither applying repeated shocks nor casually merging similar events.

  5. 5

    For concurrency, check commutation, resources, and effects on conditions, specifying the permitted domain and intermediate states.

  6. 6

    When arbitrary combination is impossible, retain order or concurrency branches and output uncertainty ranges and discriminating evidence.

Distinctions to keep clear

Evidence update

Revising judgments about past or current states today.

≠

Mechanism advancement

Estimating subsequent changes from a state according to rules.

Message-arrival order

Affected by transmission and processing delays.

≠

Actual causal order

Requires event-time and channel evidence; neither order can be directly inferred from the other.

Multiple sources

Multiple records or relays.

≠

Multiple events

Distinguishable actual occurrences, which may be interdependent; check event identity and deduplication.

A final field is identical

Local results happen to agree.

≠

Complete operations may be combined arbitrarily

Also requires no conflicts in resources, conditions, or other key states.

Correct dependent branches

Repair relevant judgments.

≠

Every conclusion becomes invalid

Local results independent of the erroneous source remain.

Mathematical construction: operation order changes the answerTeaching scenario

AssumptionsOperation definitions, absence of other updates, and overlapping windows are teaching assumptions; no real probabilities for the two orders are given.

A fictional state x starts at 1, with f(x)=x+1 and g(x)=2x. Applying f then g gives g(f(1))=4; applying g then f gives f(g(1))=3, so the operations do not commute. If evidence establishes only that both occurred in overlapping windows with unknown order, the final candidates are {3,4}; whichever tool message returns first cannot select the answer.

BoundaryCoincidence at a particular initial value or agreement in one field also cannot generally establish commutation.

Teaching construction: different fields may still compete for one resourceTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe window, indivisibility, inability to parallelize, and capacity are constructed premises; no real staffing arrangement or authorization exists.

Fictional tasks A and B each need one on-duty worker continuously for one hour and must finish within the same hour. Only one worker is available, cannot work in parallel, and neither task can be split. Their completion flags occupy different fields and appear independently updatable to complete; once shared capacity is included, both cannot finish within the window. Retain branches prioritizing A or B, or another actually feasible schedule.

BoundaryDifferent fields do not guarantee independent resources; adding staff next hour also cannot restore a completion window already missed.

Teaching construction: a local source correction does not erase independent recordsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe fictional evidence explicitly specifies E1's error, no other inventory changes, and temperature evidence independent of E1. Real dependencies require checking; different names alone do not establish independence.

A fictional inventory is 5. Report E1, ‘2 were taken yesterday,’ produces knowledge version V1 with inventory 3 and subsequent predictions based on it. An independent system has its own reliable temperature record of 20. Today E1 is verified as erroneous; append correction V2, restore the inventory estimate to 5, and recalculate dependent projections. Temperature 20 is not revoked by the unrelated E1 correction. Updating the model today does not physically add 2 items back to the world.

BoundaryCorrecting knowledge is not new physical replenishment. If the original removal was real and items were later returned, record a separate real event.

Snow records deaths and registration at different timesDocumented case

Snow's 1855 book explains that some deaths in the relevant area during the first two days of September 1854 were not registered until the following week. Death records from hospitals and other locations also required distinctions in data scope. This section uses only the first fact to show that actual event time and record-creation time cannot be collapsed into one clock.

SourceJohn Snow, 1855 second editionOriginal printed pp.40–41, the paragraph containing ‘not registered till the week following’ in the Broad Street outbreak discussionReading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThis is Snow's retrospective reconstruction of registration delays. This lesson lacks model-entry times for individual death records, does not equate death dates with infection dates, and does not calculate transmission parameters for the entire epidemic.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleTwo operations have close timestamps, so they may be processed arbitrarily in return order.

What it limitsCommutativity, resources, and conditions require checking; the f/g construction gives different consequences.

Teaching counterexampleTwo news reports say work stopped yesterday, so the model should apply two stoppages.

What it limitsFirst check whether they concern the same candidate event; more material does not mean more real occurrences.

Teaching counterexampleCorrecting an inventory message requires withdrawing an independent temperature record.

What it limitsRecomputation follows dependencies; independent local facts should not be collaterally deleted.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • Late facts must not be fed back into old prediction information sets; replay is valuable but has a different status.
  • Regenerating a model narrative alone is not a new real event or observation.
  • Deduplication does not delete sources; retain source lineage and grounds for merging. Similar events may genuinely occur more than once.
  • Executor completion order cannot be treated as real causal order.
  • Arbitrary combination is conditionally permissible, not the default for every near-simultaneous event.

Scope and open questions

The same primary historical material explicitly distinguishes death occurrence from registration time, illustrating late-arriving material. This section adds the record-clock perspective rather than the effect of handle removal.

  • Actual event merging and concurrent order require specific logs, sources, and resource material; the historical case lacks each item's model-entry time, so no complete three-time table may be fabricated.

11.4The Nine-Step Projection Loop ​

In briefThe nine steps connect a dynamic analysis: establish its starting point, explain how events change conditions, and let real outcomes correct earlier judgments. They do not guarantee that reality follows the diagram or require filling nine boxes with invented knowledge.
11.4Note

Understanding this section

11.4 Nine-step projection loop

The nine steps connect a dynamic analysis: establish its starting point, explain how events change conditions, and let real outcomes correct earlier judgments. They do not guarantee that reality follows the diagram or require filling nine boxes with invented knowledge.

This parent section contains only a navigational heading; substantive requirements lie in nine subsections. Step one freezes the starting point; two checks actors and circles; three separates M and Ψ by task; four declares clocks and channel constraints. These prepare a checkable starting point and grounds for propagation, not replaceable by an attractive relationship diagram.

Step five registers actual status of events or actions; six analyzes changes along supported channels; seven preserves branches at genuine uncertainties; eight records signals, residuals, and candidates; nine adds write-back from later actual outcomes. Each output becomes a bounded premise for later judgments; completing the procedure does not make false premises true.

A closed loop does not feed expected outcomes back as starting evidence. Save the old run, then incorporate new material in a new version; otherwise what was said at the time and comparison with a simple baseline cannot be recovered. Actual outcomes may support local paths without automatically certifying every mechanism.

These nine steps organize event projection. The book's XK0–XK11 is a broader analytical process, IG's seven gates address thresholds such as individual generation, and dynamic eligibility has its own checks. Counts cannot be merged merely because they are called steps, nor can finishing nine steps imply passing every gate.

The explanations use an explicitly fictional repair queue throughout: 6 pending items at 08:00, originally 2 arrivals and 3 processed per hour. Personnel, events, and later readings are teaching stipulations, not a business investigation. Sharing the starting point across subsections compares responsibilities; it does not turn one construction into several empirical cases. Apollo 13 material is separately inserted as bounded historical evidence, without claiming participants used Xikari or empirical superiority of the nine steps.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First check the starting point, objects, channels, and time/resource constraints, avoiding progression on unsettled premises.

  2. 2

    Register events as facts or proposals, matching propagation edges to sources individually.

  3. 3

    Retain branches that change outcomes and specify signals distinguishing them.

  4. 4

    Append actual outcomes after the old run, compare deviations and baselines, and decide local revisions.

Distinctions to keep clear

Nine-step loop

The dynamic-analysis working sequence specified here.

≠

Nine steps completed means correct

No such guarantee: evidence may be missing, mechanisms wrong, or boundaries exceeded.

Write-back

New records preserving the starting point and old predictions.

≠

Backward leakage

Presenting later-known information as known at the earlier time.

Construction spanning sections

The same fictional system illustrates different responsibilities.

≠

Independent empirical replication

Requires real and correspondingly independent observations.

Teaching construction: a complete procedure can still yield unknownTeaching scenario

AssumptionsEach hour counts arrivals before processing; no losses or other actions; processing capacity stays fixed over the two hours. All are constructed.

If the repair queue's 08:00 state and arrival rate are known but actual processing is only known to be either 1 or 3 items/hour, the queue after two hours is respectively 8 or 4. The nine steps can explicitly preserve both branches and arrange a capacity check; procedural completeness does not automatically make the answer 6.

BoundaryTwo branches do not imply 50% probability each; midpoint 6 is not established as a possible terminal value in this model.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleOnce all nine steps contain text, the system has eliminated unknowns.

What it limitsFormal completeness is not sufficient discriminating evidence; both branches remain.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • The source parent section contains no separate empirical theorem; do not fabricate a proof for it.
  • The nine steps may yield bounded scenarios, unknowns, or stopping outcomes; neither point predictions nor real actions are mandatory.

Scope and open questions

The parent contains only a navigational heading, not an independent empirical claim; historical evidence belongs in applicable subsections rather than repeated narrative accumulation.

  2. 2

Why cannot 4 and 8 be averaged into prediction 6 in this example?

No branch probabilities or grounds for the midpoint being feasible exist; retain conditional branches.
