11.9.4Early Stopping ​

In briefDeeper projection increasingly needs clear stopping points. Stopping should leave a bounded answer—what still holds and what exceeds evidence or authority—rather than merely saying ‘too complex’ or zeroing out all previous conclusions.

Stop or downgrade if object identity or scale identity fails, key assumptions cannot be inherited, the transition mechanism falls outside its domain, the recursive interface lacks closure, or branches proliferate without signals to distinguish them. Also stop or downgrade if the results reverse across the board under small changes, residuals exceed the threshold for the intended use, a deeper order adds nothing relative to a shallower one and a simple baseline, the calibrated time window is exceeded, a boundary of rights or authorization is reached, or the third-order limit is reached. The stopping record must state what can still be said and what cannot.

11.9.4Note

Understanding this section

11.9.4 Early Stopping

Deeper projection increasingly needs clear stopping points. Stopping should leave a bounded answer—what still holds and what exceeds evidence or authority—rather than merely saying ‘too complex’ or zeroing out all previous conclusions.

The first stopping class is object/interface failure: object or scale identity changes, key assumptions cannot transfer, or recursive interfaces are not closed. If the parent model stores a team’s total resources but the child asks each person’s protected minimum share, a total-only interface may fail. Continuing loses necessary task distinctions. Expand representation, downgrade to a range, or stop instead of forcing an answer from the old model.

The second class is insufficient mechanisms or discrimination: transitions exceed the domain, branches explode without distinguishing signals, tiny changes reverse conclusions throughout, or residuals exceed use thresholds. Many branches alone need not stop work if distinguishing material allows bounded checks. Sensitivity also does not mean nothing is known; local ranges or common constraints may remain.

The third class is absent increment and calibration overreach: deeper orders add no task gain over shallower orders and a simple baseline, or exceed supported calibration horizons. More computation is not justification. Short-window calibration cannot extend the same ‘90%’ into the distant future; downgrade to conditional scenarios instead of maintaining false precision.

The fourth class concerns rights and authorization. If further analysis needs unauthorized personal material or actual actions, stop that dependent path while preserving lawfully answerable parts. Recommendations, organizing unknowns, and nonintrusive formal analysis are not automatically execution; research value likewise confers no right to bypass authority.

The original also sets a third-order ceiling for this organization of exploration. Stop or downgrade there rather than continuing self-amplification to fill a fourth order; this says neither that the world has only three layers nor that third-order analysis is inherently correct. Any key stopping condition may require stopping sooner, without completing every step.

A stopping record should give triggering facts, affected branches/tasks, remaining bounded results, prohibited extrapolations, and material needed to reopen. Suspension is not permanent unknowability, and retirement does not erase historical results; genuinely new material permits reevaluation in a new version.

This responsibility connects to general stopping in 11.10 and choice stopping in 12.15, but here the focus is reentry depth and interfaces. One failed recursive branch does not automatically revoke independently known stock, actual events, or a qualified short-term total effect; preserving local knowledge is central to a stopping report.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Before every reentry, check object identity, inherited assumptions, mechanism domain, and interface closure.

  2. 2

    Check discriminating signals, sensitivity, residuals, and deeper-order increment over shallower analysis/baselines.

  3. 3

    Check horizons, rights, authority, and the third-order ceiling; stop or downgrade at any key boundary.

  4. 4

    Record remaining bounded answers, unavailable claims, and reopening material without clearing independently known results.

Distinctions to keep clear

Stop deeper projection

No further extrapolation under insufficient conditions.

≠

Deny all upstream knowledge

Independently established bounded facts remain.

Highly sensitive model

Small changes can alter conclusions.

≠

Impossible to study

Reversal conditions can still be reported and discriminating observations designed.

Third-order ceiling

A stopping rule for the current organization of exploration.

≠

The world has only three orders

The original makes no such ontological claim.

Downgrade to scenarios

Remove unsupported probabilities or certainty.

≠

Delete all outputs

Explicit conditional consequences and risk descriptions may remain.

Teaching construction: limit the answer when the interface is insufficientTeaching scenario

AssumptionsPeople, resources, and minimum shares are constructed; no actual personal data were collected.

The parent state stores only two people’s total resources, 10, while the next-order task requires at least 3 each. Distribution (5,5) satisfies it and (9,1) does not; total 10 cannot distinguish them. Stop the definite inference that everyone meets the minimum while retaining total 10. Reopening needs appropriate authorized distribution material, or a different question depending only on the total.

BoundaryDo not invent 5 per person because the total is sufficient, or revoke the known total because distribution is unknown.

Mathematical construction: tiny parameter differences reverse the conclusionTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe θ interval and threshold are teaching assumptions, with no probability distribution or measurement performed.

Let fictional binary output y=1 if θ≥0 and y=0 otherwise; only θ∈[−0.01,0.01] is known. Opposite sides of the permitted domain produce different outputs, so no robust direction follows. Report reversal threshold 0 and answer set {0,1}, stopping unique-outcome extrapolation. Only new reliable material establishing θ≥0 can narrow the model answer to 1.

BoundaryA denser parameter grid shows the reversal more clearly but does not establish which side actual θ lies on.

Teaching construction: retain earlier parts at the ceilingTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAll three orders are model-organization proposals; no schedule or institutional change occurred.

A fictional first order calculates one-hour backlog 7 under given capacity; a second order builds only an ‘if scheduling is changed’ branch; third-order institutional change still lacks key material. Stop further reentry, retaining the first-order conditional value and second-order option conditions. Do not turn third-order uncertainty into inevitable institutional improvement or erase first-order arithmetic.

BoundaryKnown one-hour conditions do not support a ten-year path; deeper futures need new tasks and corresponding material, not continued generation in the old run.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleThe third order cannot be answered reliably, so every first-order result must be withdrawn.

What it limitsWithdraw only parts dependent on failed conditions; retain independently bounded results.

Teaching counterexampleWe have not reached the third order, so we should continue despite needing unauthorized material.

What it limitsAuthority and protection boundaries may require immediate stopping; order count is no excuse.

What does not follow

  • Do not treat authorization gaps as mere computational shortages.
  • Missing long-term evidence does not establish the opposite long-term conclusion.
  • Complexity, sensitivity, and residual thresholds must match use and protection responsibilities; do not change gates ad hoc to preserve a conclusion.

Scope and open questions

This section sets stopping and downgrading thresholds for recursive models; formal examples test interface sufficiency and sensitivity. No calibration windows or authority records for actual multilevel models were obtained, and no stopping-experiment effects are fabricated.

11.10Stopping Conditions for a Projection Run ​

In briefStopping does not conceal analysis; it makes the defensible scope explicit. When one bridge fails, stop paths depending on it first. When the shared starting point of every path is wrong, stop all relevant runs.

Affected propositions and the paths that depend on them should be suspended or downgraded if a key object lacks grounds for object facts or a grouping-gain claim on which a path depends is not supported, the event’s factual status is unclear, a propagation channel is missing, a cross-scale mapping fails, or the number of paths grows without signals to distinguish them. The same rule applies if the model is extremely sensitive to small changes in parameters, privacy or safety risks exceed the value of the information, the projection is asked to generate a diagnosis, punishment, or authorization directly, or a simple baseline already performs as well or better. If a shared premise or the overall conditions for use fail, all related runs stop.

Stopping is part of the output. It must not be used to conceal failure. The stopping record should state where the projection stopped, what has been obtained, which unknowns prevent continuation, which next observation would be most informative, and what risk further projection would add.

11.10Note

Understanding this section

11.10 Stopping Conditions for Projection Runs

Stopping does not conceal analysis; it makes the defensible scope explicit. When one bridge fails, stop paths depending on it first. When the shared starting point of every path is wrong, stop all relevant runs.

This section distinguishes local and shared premises. Insufficient support for object facts or grouping gain, unclear events, missing channels, or failed cross-scale mappings first affect dependent propositions. Other independently recorded facts may remain; if shared premises fail, such as misidentified objects or an unreliable overall evidence source, stop all dependent runs. Neither stop everything mechanically nor divide a global failure into local pieces to preserve conclusions.

When a key object lacks bounded support, stop propositions treating it as established while retaining analyst-proposed groupings and existing documentary facts. If event occurrence is unverified, stop definite real-consequence claims, retaining explicit if-branches where appropriate. A missing propagation channel prevents explaining that transmission but need not revoke an independently identified terminal total effect.

Cross-scale mapping often fails when group means fill individual states or local mechanisms are directly extended to institutional outcomes. Downgrade to the scale actually supported, explaining missing aggregation, representation, or transmission relations instead of giving a larger graph automatically stronger explanatory authority.

Growing paths without discriminating signals add stories but no help for the question; extreme sensitivity to tiny parameters removes support for a unique answer. Report thresholds and answer ranges first, seek the observation most likely to change the answer, and stop if safe discrimination is impossible. The original does not prohibit branching; it rejects expansion without discriminatory value.

When privacy or safety risks exceed information value, ‘more complete collection’ cannot justify continuation. Information value is not merely a price: rights boundaries and irreversible harms may forbid offset by total benefit. Stop uses demanding projection directly produce diagnoses, punishments, or authorization; nondiagnostic information organization, questions needed for lawful procedures, and boundaries may remain, without deciding for qualified parties.

If a simple baseline performs equally well or better, stop claiming gain from complex projection; consider returning to the baseline or limiting the complex model to exploration. Comparisons need matched targets, windows, information sets, and scoring. One loss does not make all complex models forever useless, and richer stories do not excuse ignoring testable performance.

A stopping record gives five core answers: where stopping occurs, what was obtained, which unknowns prevent continuation, which next observation has greatest information value, and what risks continuation adds. ‘Most valuable’ is relative to the current question and permitted scope; discrimination alone cannot prioritize unnecessary private material.

Stopping or downgrading preserves old runs, sources, and dependencies. New material permits review in a new version; regenerating the same narrative is no reopening basis. This complements 11.9.4’s recursive stopping: that section particularly limits reentry depth, while this one covers applicability and use in any dynamic run.

Stopping conditions target dependencies on object facts, grouping gain, and mechanism channels separately. Unsupported circle gain may stop dependent complex projection or prompt simpler representation while independently established object facts remain reportable. If event identity, object K, or shared material is wrong, stop every path depending on that shared premise.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Locate failed premises and affected dependencies, first distinguishing local branches from shared premises.

  2. 2

    Determine which statements need suspension or downgrading by object, event, channel, scale, and discrimination.

  3. 3

    Check risk, use, and authority; do not substitute projection for diagnosis, punishment, or authorization.

  4. 4

    Compare baselines fairly and remove unsupported gain claims.

  5. 5

    Create the five-part stopping record and specify new material permitting reopening.

Distinctions to keep clear

Local stopping

Stop only propositions and paths dependent on failed premises.

≠

Stop all relevant runs

Applies when shared premises or overall use conditions fail.

Stop the gain claim

The complex model has not outperformed a reasonable baseline.

≠

The model is entirely worthless

Other uses such as explanation and exploration require separate evaluation.

Information is discriminating

May change the analytical answer.

≠

It may be collected

Still requires necessity, authority, and protection conditions.

Provide procedural material

Organize facts, questions, and bounded analysis.

≠

Diagnose, punish, or authorize

Qualification to decide does not arise from projection.

Teaching construction: one false message recalculates only dependent branchesTeaching scenario

AssumptionsIndependence of material and error scope are explicitly stipulated; no actual warehousing action occurs.

A fictional warehouse has measured stock 10 and an independent temperature record 20. Report E predicts resupply 5, producing modeled tomorrow stock 15 and downstream allocation branches. E is later confirmed misissued. Stop or withdraw 15 and allocation inferences dependent on resupply, retaining measured 10 and independent temperature 20. If both sensors and the report later prove to use the wrong object ID shared by the whole model’s object identification, suspend the relevant runs together.

BoundaryActual independence cannot be inferred merely from different field names; check real sources and dependencies.

Mathematical construction: equal baseline performance cannot be beaten by complexityTeaching scenario

AssumptionsPredictions, outcomes, and scoring are teaching constructions; two samples cannot establish long-term statistical equivalence.

Two fictional frozen models predict (4,6) for two targets, with actual outcomes (5,5). Regardless of the complex model’s node count, both have mean absolute error (|4−5|+|6−5|)/2=1. This use has no evidence of predictive increment; separate explanatory uses require their own evidence, not counting nodes as accuracy.

Boundary‘Equal this time’ does not rigorously prove equal future performance; it limits only gain claims supported by this material.

Teaching construction: a complete stopping entryTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe complete entry is a teaching proposal; no actual logistics query or commitment was sent.

Location: stock→timely-delivery path. Obtained: reliable initial stock 10. Unknown: whether transport is open. Block: no usable channel material, so next-day arrival cannot be asserted. Next observation: check corresponding transport status and window within existing authority. Continuation risk: treating unknown as open may create unfulfillable commitments. Give only ‘arrival is possible if the channel is open and delay≤window’, without actually promising or dispatching.

BoundaryAn independent local task unaffected by the channel may continue its analysis.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleThe resupply report was false, so independent temperature 20 must also be deleted.

What it limitsNo dependency means no collateral erasure; stopping scope follows sources and mechanisms.

Teaching counterexampleThe global object ID is wrong; pausing one graph node suffices.

What it limitsFailed shared object premises require stopping all relevant dependent runs.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleBoth models have equal error, but the complex graph looks more professional, so foresight capability improved.

What it limitsComplexity and foresight increment differ; test under the same contract.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • Local gaps do not erase independent knowledge; failed shared premises cannot be handled by stopping only one twig.
  • Baseline comparisons and stopping thresholds must be predetermined or reasonably explicit, not arbitrarily changed after results.
  • Unresolved records are part of the deliverable and should not be hidden at delivery.
  • Stopping an unauthorized use does not mean refusing every permissible information service.

Scope and open questions

This is a stopping contract for runs and uses. Constructions directly show dependency scope and baseline comparisons. Complete dependencies and authority material for an actual system were not obtained, so no stopping verdict or professional diagnosis is invented for it.

When must all relevant runs stop?

When shared premises or overall use conditions fail and relevant paths all depend on them, not whenever any local unknown occurs.

11.11An Example of a Cross-Circle Cascade ​

In briefThis is not an investigation of an actual company but the original text's continuing public-resignation teaching scenario. It lays out possible paths through the team, management, family, professional community, and platform, focusing on where conditions break rather than choosing a path for the company.

Continue with the public departure from a job in Part 10. The starting snapshot shows that the employee faces long working hours and the pressure of care work, team trust is declining, company management is concerned with reputation, the professional community provides outside opportunities, and public opinion on the platform has yet to form. The event is the employee publishing an account of their departure. Part of its content can be verified, and part is personal narrative.

Direct effects include the team receiving the information, the platform obtaining a text that can be circulated, and management facing pressure to respond. On the first path, the company makes only a public denial. In the short term, external public opinion may branch toward either fading or amplification. If members inside the company interpret the denial as suppression, team trust declines and further departures occur through bridges in the professional community. On the second path, the company acknowledges the problem and starts verifiable adjustments to resources and appeals. If these are carried out, working hours and processes change on the organizational clock. Trust may recover more slowly on the experience–meaning clock. On the third path, changes in family care conditions ease the employee’s pressure after leaving. This does not directly change the team’s state unless the employee continues to bridge information or resources.

Early signals can include the number of internal appeals, records of hours actually worked, members’ public statements, and changes in hiring and departures. Contrary signals can include no actual change in resources after a policy is announced, increasing internal silence despite declining external exposure, or the professional community failing to form a bridge. Residuals may come from the states of key managers, the platform’s recommendation mechanism, or unobserved legal constraints. These enter only the ledger of variable candidates.

The projection still cannot say which path the company “should” take. It provides conditional consequences and signals that distinguish the paths. Forecast registration, comparison of options, normative premises, and authorization are addressed in the next Part.

11.11Note

Understanding this section

11.11 An example of a cross-circle cascade

This is not an investigation of an actual company but the original text's continuing public-resignation teaching scenario. It lays out possible paths through the team, management, family, professional community, and platform, focusing on where conditions break rather than choosing a path for the company.

Long hours, care pressure, declining team trust, management's reputational concerns, and community opportunities are all original scenario assumptions, not researcher measurements. Unformed platform public opinion is also just the starting premise. §10.11 first draws the joint objects and dual channels; this section injects publication of a resignation statement to show conditional branching of subsequent states.

The resignation statement contains checkable facts and personal narrative with different support scopes. Relevant working-hours, institutional-text, or handoff-record components may be independently verified. Feelings are material about the person's experience and claims, neither categorically noise nor substitutes for others' inner states or every fact of the event. No specific text is supplied here, so accusations, dialogue, and legal conclusions cannot be invented.

Direct effects also need separate channels: team receipt is arrival; platform receipt of the text creates propagatable material; pressure on management to respond is a stipulated consequence. Propagatability is not wide propagation, nor receipt belief. Actual applications must separately check visibility, responses, and subsequent states.

Path one begins with public denial: external attention may subside briefly or intensify. Further resignations along this branch require internal members to interpret denial as suppression, trust to fall further, and the professional community to create actual opportunity bridges. Every “if” bears independent evidential responsibility. Public denial is not automatically suppression, nor is everyone's interpretation identical.

Path two begins with acknowledgment and verifiable adjustments, distinguishing promises from execution. Only actual changes to resources and appeal procedures allow registration of working-hours and process changes on the organizational clock. Experience–meaning trust may recover more slowly or not at all. Better announcement wording does not establish resources in place, and resources in place do not automatically establish repaired meaning.

Path three improves family-care conditions, potentially reducing post-resignation pressure and changing the employee's available actions. It does not directly change the team. Further return requires channels such as continued information or resource bridging. The original avoids coloring the whole company as improved from one person's better state.

The three paths are neither mutually exclusive nor exhaustive histories. Family conditions may improve alongside company denial or actual adjustment. Management may deny first and reform later; create time- and evidence-specific nodes rather than compress all actions into one moment. These are meaningful mechanism entry points, with other supported paths possible in reality.

Early signals include changes in appeals, working-hours implementation, public expression, recruitment, and resignation. Each needs windows, denominators, and record-generation processes. More appeals may mean more problems or greater willingness to report through improved channels. Public silence may mean no objection, fear, platform exit, or something else. One indicator cannot decide every mechanism.

Contrary signals must target paths: a published policy without resource changes weakens “adjustment implemented”; reduced exposure with increased internal silence does not establish repaired trust; absent actual professional-community bridging blocks that opportunity-transmission segment. Contrary material weakens a specific explanation without automatically proving opposite motives.

Key managers' states, recommendation mechanisms, and legal constraints remain residual candidates. Without actual measurements or legal material, this section fills in no personalities, algorithm parameters, or responsibility verdicts. Projection yields conditional consequences and distinguishing signals only. “Which should be chosen” additionally needs normative premises, option comparison, and foresight responsibilities; execution further requires valid authorization.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Label the whole example an original teaching scenario, separating assumptions, checkable fact types, and personal narrative.

  2. 2

    Enter subsequent conditional paths separately from information receipt, available text, and response pressure.

  3. 3

    Check internal interpretations, actual resource adjustments, opportunity bridges, and family spillovers segment by segment. Arrival is not effect.

  4. 4

    Register positive/contrary signals and competing explanations in different windows, retaining parallel paths.

  5. 5

    Residuals enter only the candidate ledger. Normative preferences and execution require explicit conditions and authorization procedures.

Distinctions to keep clear

Original scenario assumption

A fictional starting point illustrating an analytical method.

≠

Actual company-investigation conclusion

Requires actual material absent from this section.

Public denial

An observable form of response.

≠

Members interpret it as suppression

A meaning judgment with its own positions and material, not an automatic equivalence.

More appeals

Observed counts rise.

≠

Problems necessarily worsen

Recording channels and reporting tendencies may also change.

Reduced family pressure

Improved conditions for the individual employee.

≠

Simultaneous team improvement

Requires separate bridging and transmission mechanisms.

Conditional consequences

What follows if path conditions hold.

≠

Ought or authorized

Requires normative comparison and independent authorization.

Reading branches in the original teaching scenarioTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAnnouncement and resource arrangements are teaching additions to the original fictional scenario, referring to no actual company.

If a company announces a new appeal channel without changing budget, on-duty personnel, or processing authority, register only the announcement and its arrival. “Actual appeal-uptake capacity improved” remains to be checked. If later actual records show resources in place, update the corresponding organizational state without waiting for everyone's trust to recover before acknowledging resource changes.

BoundaryObtain separate evidence for resources and trust; lack of verification for one cannot categorically negate the other.

Mathematical construction: appeal counts depend on reporting channelsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsCoverage proportions here are exact aggregate recording fractions, not random sample realizations passed off as expectations. Problem counts and proportions are fictional.

Suppose each of two fictional weeks has 20 actual unresolved problems. In week one exactly 1/4 enter the records, yielding 5; in week two 1/2 enter, yielding 10. Doubled observed appeals do not mean doubled problems. With unknown recording probabilities, changed counts may also include changed problems; one cannot conclude everything merely reflects improved channels.

BoundaryActual use must check definitions, denominators, duplicates, and selection. This example does not deny that actual problems may increase.

Teaching construction: the family branch can run in parallel without direct spilloverTeaching scenario

AssumptionsExit and bridging status are stipulated. No care details are requested from actual families.

A fictional employee gains caregiving support and more discretionary time each week while the company continues public denial. If the employee has left the team and transmits no further information or resources, this model has no edge from family improvement directly to team trust. If the professional community later creates a new bridge, new material must establish a separate path.

BoundaryAbsence of the specified edge limits only this explanation, not all possible actual indirect connections.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexamplePublic exposure falls, so internal trust must have recovered.

What it limitsExternal visibility differs from internal meaning. Silence and exposure each have competing explanations.

Teaching counterexampleThe company says adjustment began, so working hours and appeal resources should immediately be marked improved.

What it limitsAn initiation statement is not actual execution; corresponding records are required.

Teaching counterexampleCare pressure decreases, so the company's team state automatically improves.

What it limitsA specific bridging channel is required; individual changes do not directly fill collective states.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • The original three branches supply no actual occurrence probabilities. Enumeration counts are not probabilities.
  • One event may produce opposite outcomes in different circles. External exposure is not a proxy for internal trust.
  • Unperformed resource changes cannot be recorded as complete. No actual personnel or legal disposition is executed in this example.
  • Resignation does not diagnose personality, nor are personal choices entirely dissolved into structural determination.

Scope and open questions

The original explicitly continues an analytical example without an actual company, date, or primary archive. This lesson explains the teaching construction without inventing real people, accusations, working hours, or platform data. External cases cannot replace passage-by-passage explanation of the original example.

  • Actual application requires the resignation text, checkable records, accounts from different positions, actual resource execution, and bridging material, respecting purpose, privacy, and authorization boundaries.

11.12Outputs of This Part ​

In briefA projection deliverable cannot consist only of a final route map. Readers should see starting points, events, assumptions, stepwise changes, unknowns, and stopping points, and know which elements are conditional preparation and which lack forecasting or action eligibility.

A qualifying projection output should include a frozen joint snapshot, event type and evidence, mechanism and parameter assumptions, update steps, and a path graph. For every path, it should record conditions, clocks, support status, and early and contrary signals. It should also include residuals and variable candidates, stopping conditions, a plan for writing back results, and an explicit statement separating prediction and action.

Projection can improve structured preparation for what follows, but it remains conditional. Without registration before results, a simple baseline, calibration, and continuing write-back, it cannot support a claim that foresight capability has improved. Without normative grounds and authorization, it cannot support a claim that an action should be carried out. An analysis based on explicit normative premises can recommend an option, reject it, or recommend deferral. None of these judgments establishes that the option has been authorized for execution. For each such judgment, its grounds, costs, opposing case, and conditions for revision must be stated in full.

11.12Note

Understanding this section

11.12 Outputs of this part

A projection deliverable cannot consist only of a final route map. Readers should see starting points, events, assumptions, stepwise changes, unknowns, and stopping points, and know which elements are conditional preparation and which lack forecasting or action eligibility.

The frozen joint snapshot specifies object, task, scale, time, evidence cutoff, and key states. Event types and evidence distinguish actual occurrence, reports, plans, and simulations; mechanism and parameter assumptions specify propagation dependencies. Without these three entry points, it is hard to tell whether later paths derive from the same start or switch premises segment by segment.

Update steps and the path graph jointly explain how changes occur. Each path retains conditions, clocks, support status, and early/contrary signals rather than merely “success” or “failure.” Ungrounded probabilities remain unassigned; a complete graph does not require invented numbers. Path lineage and identity continue under preceding contracts.

Residuals and variable candidates expose unexplained areas. Stopping conditions state when extrapolation ends. The outcome write-back plan specifies how future material will be compared with the original run and baseline. Plans are not observed outcomes; a completed write-back field does not mean learning occurred.

Projection helps structured preparation for changing conditions, but “improved foresight capability” is a separate testable claim requiring registration before outcomes, a reasonable simple baseline, corresponding calibration, and continuing write-back. Without these, say only that paths and signals for checking were organized, not that predictions improved. Where material supports a local conclusion, procedural modesty should not prevent a clear answer.

Explain prediction, normative judgment, and execution authority separately. Likelier occurrence does not imply something should be brought about. Under explicit normative premises, analysis may recommend, veto, or defer, fully stating evidence, costs, the opposing case, and revision conditions. Such deliberative judgment does not automatically receive actual execution authority.

“No claim that action should be executed without norms and authorization” does not mean analysts can never recommend. Norms premise comparison of goals, floors, and distribution; authorization determines who may implement actual actions. Missing execution permission still permits an analytical preference with gaps stated, but the two statuses must remain distinct. The next part separates prediction registration from option selection in detail.

Complete output is necessary for checkability, not sufficient for theoretical or empirical correctness. A file with every field may still contain faulty observations, mismatched mechanisms, or uncovered risks. Conversely, explicitly marking necessary fields inapplicable or unknown is better than filling them without grounds.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Retain frozen snapshots, input statuses, and mechanism parameters so the starting point remains traceable.

  2. 2

    Display update steps, path graphs, and each branch's conditions/clocks/support/positive and contrary signals.

  3. 3

    List residual candidates, stopping conditions, and the write-back plan for actual outcomes when they arrive.

  4. 4

    Declare separately conditional preparation, predictive-capability evaluation, normative opinions, and execution-authorization status.

  5. 5

    Fully explain recommendation grounds, costs, objections, and revision conditions. Complete delivery does not replace factual testing.

Distinctions to keep clear

Structured preparation

Knowing which conditions change paths and what to observe.

≠

Established foresight gain

Requires a prior contract, baseline, and outcome evaluation.

Write-back plan

A commitment about comparing future material.

≠

Completed write-back

Actual outcomes have arrived and changed corresponding records.

Analytical preference

A deliberative opinion under explicit norms and evidence.

≠

Authorized execution

Requires separate valid authority, not automatically generated by preference.

Complete fields

Content is locatable and checkable.

≠

Correct conclusion

Still requires support from facts, mechanisms, and applicability conditions.

Teaching construction: a minimal but substantive projection summaryTeaching scenario

AssumptionsNumbers, event, and rules are teaching assumptions; no actual system was operated.

The object is a fictional repair queue, frozen at 08:00 with B=6 and arrivals of 2/hour. The event is “if equipment slows,” not an event already occurring. The rule is next B=max(0,B+2−c), with assumed c=1 or 3. One-step path A gives 7 at 09:00, path B gives 5; the clock is one hour, support is conditional derivation, and no probabilities are supplied. The early signal is actual completions in the same window; the contrary signal is a record corresponding to the other capacity. Both branches share a starting point and are mutually exclusive. No actual reading yet permits residual calculation; the candidate set is empty, not numerical zero. Stop at 09:00 or when channel/object/permission conditions fail. The write-back plan is to obtain actual records with matching definitions, compare absolute error against the prespecified persistence baseline 6, and append a version. Separation statement: no predictive-gain score exists, and no repair or scheduling action is executed.

BoundaryReal-world support for candidate c is unknown and subsequent records have not arrived; “calibrated” or “zero residual” must not be recorded in advance.

Teaching construction: conditional recommendation is not executionTeaching scenario

AssumptionsEqual effects and risks are strong teaching assumptions, not a claim that real options require only financial comparison.

In another fictional comparison, option A costs 2 and B costs 5; all relevant effects and risks are stipulated equal, and the explicit norm is “choose lower cost when the same protection conditions are met.” A may be analytically preferred because it costs 3 less. The counterargument is unexamined hidden maintenance cost; revision conditions are A's additional costs exceeding 3 or differing protection conditions. No actual permissions are supplied, so the advice remains for deliberation, without purchasing or scheduling.

BoundaryThe preference cannot be copied without explicit values or comparative evidence; cost definitions and rights floors also require actual verification.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleA snapshot and path diagram exist, so foresight capability has improved.

What it limitsWithout preregistration and outcome/baseline evaluation, this is organizational preparation, not evidence of gain.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleWithout execution authority, even a conditional preference cannot be proposed.

What it limitsAdvice for deliberation may be offered where evidence and explicit norms permit, retaining the permission gap.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleResults have not arrived, so enter 0 for the residual to complete the table.

What it limitsNot yet calculable means unknown or not applicable, not zero difference.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • Do not invent parameters, measurements, or authorization to fill every field.
  • A preference with objections and costs is still a position. State the conditional judgment clearly.
  • Later factual changes require appended versions, not overwriting the original run.

Scope and open questions

This section is a normative checklist of deliverable contents and uses. A minimal complete construction can test the fields' roles; unrelated real stories are unnecessary as supposed proof of correctness.

11.13Action Choice and Updating Conditions ​

In briefAction is more than choosing from a fixed menu. Acting changes resources, rules, relationships, and what others can do; the next step must begin from these new conditions rather than ask the model to reevaluate the same old menu.

For dynamic questions involving actors, having a model evaluate a set of static options is insufficient. At each step, first use the current state to identify actions actually available, actions ruled out, and the source of the restrictions. Then analyze how an actor might choose given their information, resources, relationships, habits, and goals. Capability, belief, willingness, and actual action must be kept separate. Being able to act does not mean the actor will act. Stating an intention does not mean it has been carried out. An analyst’s recommendation does not amount to adoption by the actor.

For each choice with a basis in the material, specify which mechanism it triggers, which states change first, who is affected through which interfaces, and how these changes alter the set of actions available at the next step. State differences must be expressed in concrete terms such as resources, rules, relationships, beliefs, or feasible actions. Feeding the same materials to another model and generating another narrative cannot substitute for updating a state. If the material does not determine the choice, retain several conditional paths. Do not decide for the actor just to continue the projection.

Later projection starts from explicitly stated conditional state differences and inherits unresolved unknowns and restrictions. When real feedback arrives, first verify its source and event status. Then compare the original path, competing paths, and the simple baseline. Distinguish factual errors, mechanism errors, different choices of action, deviations in execution, and external changes. The corrected result should change the states, parameters, scope of mechanisms, or paths used in the next round. Keeping only the text of the feedback while retaining the same choice rule does not warrant claiming that the model has learned.

11.13Note

Understanding this section

11.13 Action Choice and Conditional Updating

Action is more than choosing from a fixed menu. Acting changes resources, rules, relationships, and what others can do; the next step must begin from these new conditions rather than ask the model to reevaluate the same old menu.

At each step identify currently available and excluded actions, specifying whether limits come from capability, resources, time, relationships, institutions, or permissions. Exclusion may mean currently impossible or impermissible; distinguish them. Technically feasible unauthorized actions do not thereby enter the model's implementable action set.

Capability, belief, willingness, and actual action require separate evidence. Ability does not imply willingness; willingness does not imply belief in effectiveness; public intention does not mean execution; and an analyst's recommendation certainly does not mean adoption by the actor. Retain conditional paths for uncertain choices rather than decide for actors to advance another round.

Place possible choices within the actor's information, resources, relationships, habits, and objectives at the time. These may constrain or support strategies without completely determining the person absent identification; group tendencies also cannot fill all individual states. When anticipated responses of others change present strategy, anticipated reflexivity may be explicitly included while retaining its model-assumption status.

For each evidenced choice, specify triggering mechanisms, first changed states, transmission interfaces, affected objects and clocks, and calculate how these differences change the next action set. Concrete state differences may include reduced balances, new rule restrictions, changed relational commitments, updated beliefs, or more/fewer feasible tasks; “the system improves” is insufficient.

Later projections inherit new conditions along with unresolved unknowns and limits. Selecting a hypothetical branch does not mean reality has excluded the others; resources not yet arrived belong only in conditional branches. Giving another model the same material generates another narrative version; without new inputs, rules, or state differences, it cannot be registered as progression of the world.

When actual feedback arrives, first check source, event status, time, and duplicated underlying sources, then compare original and competing paths and simple baselines. Deviations may come from incorrect initial facts, mistaken mechanisms, an actor choosing differently, execution departing from plan, or changed external conditions. These five categories point to different revisions; not every deviation means “people are uncooperative” or “the model needs more complexity.”

Correction should change the states, parameters, mechanism scope, or paths actually used next round. Discovering that approval does not mean arrival, for example, requires revising resource availability, not merely logging “pay attention to authorization.” Saving feedback text while keeping choice rules and used states unchanged does not establish learning. Even an actual rule change still requires testing whether it improves future tasks.

This section connects dynamic projection to Part XII's choice and calibration. It automatically supplies neither value targets nor actual execution permission. Analysis may clearly identify a preferable branch or recommend delay under declared targets, while evidence, norms, feasibility, and authorization remain separately registered.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    List available and excluded actions from current conditions, distinguishing sources in capability, constraints, and permissions.

  2. 2

    Separate beliefs, willingness, and evidence of occurrence, retaining conditional branches for uncertain choices.

  3. 3

    Specify mechanisms and concrete state differences triggered by each choice, then recalculate the next feasible set.

  4. 4

    Inherit unknowns and limits; repeated generation is not state change.

  5. 5

    After verifying actual feedback, distinguish facts, mechanisms, choices, execution, and external changes; revise items actually used next round and test them separately.

Distinctions to keep clear

Able to act

Capability, resources, and other conditions make an action technically feasible.

≠

Will act or has acted

Willingness, choice, and actual occurrence each need grounds.

Different choice

The actor actually takes another available branch.

≠

Execution deviation

The chosen plan is implemented differently; this is a different error.

Evidenced concrete state update

Actual changes need factual material; simulated changes need explicit conditions, each retaining its status.

≠

Narrative version change

Rewording or redescribing with another model does not mean the state changed.

Feedback archived

Material is preserved.

≠

Next-round rule changed

The revision actually enters later use; effectiveness still requires testing.

Normative analytical recommendation

Compares options under explicit targets.

≠

Actor adoption

Actual decision and execution material cannot be replaced by a recommendation.

Mathematical construction: choice changes the next menuTeaching scenario

AssumptionsDeterministic consumption, no automatic replenishment, indivisible tasks, and corresponding operating permission are stipulated; this is not actual robot control.

A fictional robot has charge 5; task A consumes 3, B consumes 4, and permitted waiting consumes 0. Every task must leave nonnegative charge. Initially A, B, and waiting are all technically feasible. Actually doing A first leaves charge 2, making both A and B infeasible next; only waiting or a separately grounded replenishment action remains. Doing B first leaves 1, also preventing A. Treating “both tasks are feasible initially” as permission to perform both sequentially ignores shared resources.

BoundaryActual charging or resource changes must be registered before updating; replenishment cannot be presumed afterward.

Teaching construction: five deviation types must not collapse into one causeTeaching scenario

AssumptionsTeaching candidates, not events established as having occurred; several may act together.

A fictional queue predicts 5 awaiting repair next hour, but the actual record is 8. Factual error: the initial count may not have been 6. Mechanism error: processing rates may vary. Different choice: personnel selected another allowed task. Execution deviation: repair was chosen but tools did not arrive. External change: arrivals suddenly increased. These are competing diagnostic tasks, not grounds to select a cause without material. If tool nonarrival is verified, revise execution and resource states without first changing personality parameters.

BoundaryThe causal categories are neither mutually exclusive nor exhaustive; actual revision requires sources and discriminating material.

Mathematical construction: storing feedback and changing rules can be distinguished explicitlyTeaching scenario

AssumptionsActions, states, and failure records are teaching assumptions; no actual actions were executed or systems trained.

A fictional old rule chooses action a consuming 3 even when stock x=2, violating nonnegativity. After receiving a verified failure record, merely adding “be careful next time” while retaining the rule selects a again. If the allowed set becomes {a:consumption≤x} and is actually used next round, a is excluded at x=2. Rule change is checkable, but its overall performance in other future contexts still requires testing.

BoundaryProves only exclusion of a under the given constraint, not global optimality or general learning success.

2017 S3 retrospective: explicit reported changes in tool rulesDocumented case

In its retrospective of the 2017 S3 incident, AWS stated that it modified the tool to remove capacity more slowly and added safeguards preventing subsystems from falling below required minimum capacity. This section uses only the point that “revision should enter actual operating rules.”

SourceAWS incident reviewMain text paragraph 3, beginning “We are making several changes…”Reading scope: Read

Scope and limitsThe operator's report of a modified tool, not an independent audit by this lesson or proof of zero future failures. It does not establish completion of every improvement plan.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleA and B are both initially feasible, so A followed by B is also feasible.

What it limitsShared charge changes later options: 5−3=2 is insufficient for B's 4.

What it limitsIf next-round states and rules remain unchanged, archiving is not the relevant correction; even changed rules need effect validation.

Teaching counterexampleAn actual outcome differs from prediction, so the actor must lack willingness.

What it limitsFacts, mechanisms, choices, execution, and external changes are competing explanations; responsibility cannot be assigned to one cause.

What does not follow

  • Do not choose for an actor because the model requires a definite action.
  • Technical feasibility cannot override permissions; actual unauthorized behavior still enters factual records.
  • Behavioral explanation automatically neither excuses nor blames; deviations do not diagnose personality.
  • An implemented revision does not prove permanent immunity to failure; extrapolation remains bounded.

Scope and open questions

This firsthand retrospective distinguishes actual tool changes from later plans, illustrating concrete rule updating beyond recording feedback.
